headline: Railgun core upgrade and pause powers reach T1 fund-custody contracts through token governance with a 604800 second uncontested execution offset on Ethereum, but broad token distribution and all per-chain authorities were not fully verified.

findings.text: On Ethereum, the Railgun proxy owner is the Delegator, the ProxyAdmin owner is the same Delegator, and the Delegator owner is the Voting contract, so the observed Ethereum control path is Voting -> Delegator -> ProxyAdmin/proxy.
On Arbitrum, the Railgun proxy and ProxyAdmin are owned through the Arbitrum Delegator, and the Arbitrum Delegator is owned by the ArbitrumExecutor.

The core Railgun proxy is documented as an EIP1967 Transparent Upgradeable Proxy; the ProxyAdmin exposes upgrade(address,address), pause(address), unpause(address), and transferProxyOwnership(address,address), so the core fund-custody surface is upgradeable.

Ethereum governance constants read on-chain give VOTING_START_OFFSET = 172800 seconds, VOTING_YAY_END_OFFSET = 432000 seconds, VOTING_NAY_END_OFFSET = 518400 seconds, EXECUTION_START_OFFSET = 604800 seconds, and EXECUTION_END_OFFSET = 1209600 seconds after vote call; the uncontested fast path to execution is therefore 604800 seconds after callVote.
No Safe or multisig was surfaced on the fetched Ethereum or Arbitrum control path; the fetched path uses governance/executor and Delegator contracts rather than an identified multisig.

Ethereum Voting has PROPOSAL_SPONSOR_THRESHOLD = 500000 RAIL, QUORUM = 2000000 RAIL, proposalsLength = 23, and the Staking contract reports totalVotingPower about 39923789 RAIL, making quorum about 5.01% of current voting power.
The fetched proxy and ProxyAdmin sources expose pause/unpause through the same owner-governed path and show no separate emergency guardian or on-chain maximum pause duration.

The highest observed tier is T1 because ProxyAdmin.upgrade(address,address) can replace the implementation behind the fund-custody proxy and pause(address) can halt the proxy fallback/delegate path used by shield/transact/unshield; changeFee is separately bounded to at most BASIS_POINTS/2 for shield and unshield fees, but T1 upgrade/pause dominates.

steelman.red: The red case is that the ProxyAdmin can upgrade or pause a fund-custody proxy, and Polygon/BSC authority reads were incomplete, so an unobserved hot admin path cannot be excluded for every deployment.
steelman.orange: The orange case is that known Ethereum and Arbitrum T1 powers sit behind governance/executor contracts with a 604800 second execution offset, but the green requirement of broad token distribution and every per-chain authority read was not established.
steelman.green: The green case is that Ethereum control is visibly routed through token governance rather than an EOA or 2-of-3 multisig, with on-chain quorum, sponsor threshold, and a 7-day execution-start offset.

rationale.verdict: Choosing orange because the highest observed power is T1 upgrade/pause of the core proxy, the Ethereum fast-path delay reaches 604800 seconds, but broad token distribution and full Polygon/BSC authority coverage were not verified; that is stronger than red for the fetched Ethereum/Arbitrum paths, but weaker than green under the 7-day plus broad-governance standard.

headline: Core exits are on-chain through transact/unshield, but the fund-custody proxy can be paused indefinitely by governance and RAIL staking exits have a 2592000 second unlock delay.

findings.text: The main user-facing Railgun privacy-pool exit path is transact, which validates transactions and calls transferTokenOut for unshield outputs; staking exits are separate unlock(uint256) and claim(uint256) functions.

RailgunSmartWallet shield and transact are external user-facing functions without an onlyOwner/whitelist modifier in the fetched implementation source, but proxy fallback/delegate execution is guarded by the proxy-level notPaused modifier.
Staking unlock(uint256) and claim(uint256) are public user functions in the fetched Staking source and no pause modifier was observed on those functions.

The Ethereum proxy and ProxyAdmin pause path is controlled through Delegator/Voting ownership, and the fetched proxy source shows pause/unpause toggling a storage slot with no maximum pause duration or auto-expiry.
No separate fast emergency pause actor was found on the fetched Ethereum/Arbitrum paths; pause/unpause uses the same owner-governed proxy or ProxyAdmin path as upgrades.
The core Railgun privacy-pool exit is not a queued request/claim design in the fetched source; RAIL staking, however, has STAKE_LOCKTIME = 2592000 seconds between unlock and claim.
No forced-exit or escape-hatch mechanism was located that bypasses a paused proxy for Railgun privacy-pool transact/unshield.

Exit paths are directly callable on-chain: the deployed proxy ABI exposes transact, and the public Wallet SDK/Engine SDK and developer docs describe contract-interaction flows independent of the official frontend.

steelman.red: The red case is that a paused proxy blocks transact/unshield and the fetched proxy source imposes no maximum pause duration.
steelman.orange: The orange case is that the indefinite pause is routed through governance rather than a single EOA or 2-of-3 multisig, the core privacy pool has no finalized-claim stage to pause separately, and RAIL staking has a 30-day unlock queue.
steelman.green: The green case is that shield, transact, unlock, and claim are public on-chain functions and no admin signature or frontend cooperation is needed when the proxy is not paused.

rationale.verdict: Choosing orange because users can exit directly through on-chain transact/unshield and staking claim flows, but core privacy-pool exits are broadly blocked by an uncapped governance-controlled proxy pause and staking exits have a documented 2592000 second unlock delay.

headline: Impacted TVS from a protocol-introduced single external dependency appears ~0% for the assessed core: shield/transact has no oracle or bridge dependency, optional external calls are user-selected, and broadcasters are self-relayable.

findings.text: The core Railgun module assessed is the RailgunSmartWallet proxy using shield and transact; fetched source and surfacers show token transfers and user-selected cross-contract calls, but no protocol-wide oracle, price feed, AMM pool, lending pool, or staking/deposit contract dependency required for core shield/unshield accounting.

RailgunLogic external token interactions are direct user-token transfers in and out, while cross-contract calls are explicitly user-specified call targets/data and revert atomically if the external call fails.

Broadcasters are off-chain actors for relaying private transactions and paying gas, but docs state users can self-relay and that broadcasters are not needed for Shield, so broadcaster failure degrades UX/privacy rather than giving an external committee power to mint, burn, finalize, or freeze principal.

Railgun has separate deployments across chains, and the Arbitrum governance executor references retryable-ticket style L1/L2 execution, but no bridge is required for the core user flow of shielding and transacting assets already on a given chain.

Nested collateral/restaking risk is not introduced by the core Railgun design; users may shield arbitrary ERC20/ERC721 assets, so failure of a user-selected asset or external DeFi target affects that opted-in asset/transaction rather than cross-cutting Railgun accounting.

The live fallback for broadcaster dependency is self-relay; the live fallback for optional external contract-call failure is atomic revert of the user transaction rather than protocol accounting accepting a bad external result.

Railgun is deployed on third-party L1/L2 chains and is not itself an appchain or app-rollup in the fetched evidence, so L2 sequencer risk is substrate rather than a Railgun-specific autonomy dependency.
No keeper was found that must act for user funds to remain solvent; broadcasters are optional relayers for private transactions, and the docs describe self-relay as an alternative.

No specific mutable oracle, bridge endpoint, or external dependency registry was found in the assessed core contracts; generic proxy upgradeability is control-slice risk and was not counted as an autonomy A9 dependency surface.

steelman.red: The red case is that optional cross-contract calls can target arbitrary external DeFi contracts, so a malicious or broken target can harm the user-selected transaction or asset.
steelman.orange: The orange case is that broadcaster/Waku liveness and user-selected external DeFi calls can degrade privacy, UX, or expected execution, and the per-chain/per-recipe dependency census is incomplete.
steelman.green: The green case is that the core shield/transact/unshield accounting does not depend on a price oracle, non-canonical bridge, keeper, or external committee; broadcasters are self-relayable and optional external calls revert atomically.

rationale.verdict: Choosing green because the assessed core module holding the material fetched balances exposes shield/transact privacy-pool mechanics without a protocol-wide oracle, bridge, or keeper dependency, and the worst identified external touchpoints are user-selected assets/calls or optional broadcasters with self-relay fallback; module weighting is same-address proxy portfolio ~97% Ethereum and ~3% Arbitrum in the fetched explorer view, with Polygon/BSC unquantified but architecturally similar in the fetched ABIs.

Railgun docs state that shielding brings tokens into private 0zk from public 0x, shield() is the entry function, spend transactions call transact(), and all tokens share the same Merkle tree.
Railgun docs state that cross-contract calls are optional ordered calls against a private balance, can unshield, multicall, and shield back in one transaction, and failure reverts the entire call.

headline: Railgun contracts expose public shield/transact paths with no observed user KYC or address whitelist, and independent SDKs provide practical non-official-frontend access; the observed blocklist is token-level.

findings.text: The core user entry/exit functions shield and transact are external functions in the fetched implementation source and are exposed in deployed proxy ABIs; no onlyWhitelisted, onlyRole, KYC, or user-address allowlist modifier was observed on these functions.

Railgun has an owner-managed token blocklist through addToBlocklist/removeFromBlocklist and tokenBlocklist(address), but the fetched source applies this to token addresses in commitment validation rather than to user-wallet admission.

Broadcasters are in the relay path for private 0zk transactions but not an admission approver: docs say broadcasters are not needed for Shield and users can self-relay, so no single operator approval is required for core contract admission.
Fetched Railgun Labs legal and privacy pages did not provide a verbatim sanctions, KYC, or restricted-jurisdiction clause; no active official-frontend IP or wallet screening was verified in this run.

Independent access paths exist via public Wallet SDK and Engine SDK repositories and developer docs that describe node.js backends, proof generation, and direct interaction with Railgun smart contracts.

No contract-level user-address sanctions or compliance blocklist was found in the assessed core; the observed blocklist surface is tokenBlocklist(address), i.e. asset-level rather than user-address admission.
Read access is public through block explorers and DeFiPunkd surfacers, while write access to core shield/transact and staking stake/unlock/claim is public when the proxy is not paused.

The fetched legal pages were Railgun Labs legal/privacy pages; no Terms of Service page with extractable jurisdictional, sanctions, or eligibility wording was found and therefore no such clause is asserted.

steelman.red: The red case is that the protocol can blocklisted-token deposits and a relay network exists, so a careless reviewer might treat admission as operator or compliance-gated.
steelman.orange: The orange case is that the official UI posture and live relay availability were not fully tested, so practical access could be less convenient without Railgun-published clients.
steelman.green: The green case is that contract-level shield/transact admission is permissionless for users, broadcasters are bypassable by self-relay or unnecessary for Shield, and public SDKs give independent access paths.

rationale.verdict: Choosing green because the grade-setting access layer is the contract plus independent access paths: shield/transact are public in the deployed ABI/source, no user KYC/whitelist or address sanctions blocklist was observed, broadcasters do not approve admission, and public Wallet/Engine SDKs provide practical non-official-frontend access.

headline: Core proxy and implementation sources are verified and public repos/audits exist, but the current implementation has unverified Poseidon libraries and fetched audits are stale relative to current deployments.

findings.text: Ethereum core proxy 0xFA7093... is Etherscan source-code verified as a proxy and resolves to implementation 0xB4F2d77bD12c6b548Ae398244d7FAD4ABCE4D89b.

The current Ethereum implementation 0xB4F2... is Etherscan source-code verified exact match as RailgunSmartWallet, but the explorer page states it contains unverified libraries PoseidonT3 and PoseidonT4.

DeFiPunkd ABI responses show Ethereum Voting, Delegator, ProxyAdmin, and proxy ABI/source availability from etherscan or sourcify; Arbitrum and Polygon surfacers also showed ABI sources, while Polygon state reads failed.
A public Railgun contract repository exists and fetched GitHub source files correspond structurally to the deployed ABI/source names, but no deployed-bytecode-to-commit match was pinned in this run.

The fetched ABDK official-assets audit reviewed Railgun Privacy Contract code at commit 6281cb in July 2021, with scope including Commitments, RailgunLogic, Snark, TokenWhitelist, Types, and Verifier files.

The fetched Hacken official-assets audit is dated November 2 2021 and reviewed the Railgun contract repository at commit d2c63577ddd8310c87dced0d549cf9505b372111, including governance, logic, proxy, token, and treasury files.
The fetched audit firms are ABDK Consulting and Hacken; neither fetched audit is from the prompt's recognized-firm list, so the fetched audit coverage is orange-at-best for a green-grade claim.

The latest fetched audit scope is from 2021, while the current Etherscan implementation is compiled with Solidity v0.8.17 and the proxy with v0.8.12; no later fetched recognized audit or differential review was tied to the current implementation.
The proxy and implementation are not fully unverified, but implementation verification is weakened by the explorer-disclosed unverified PoseidonT3 and PoseidonT4 libraries.

steelman.red: The red case is that a verified proxy with unverified implementation libraries can block full independent bytecode verification of cryptography-critical code.
steelman.orange: The orange case is that the main proxy and implementation are source-verified and repos/audits exist, but implementation libraries are unverified and fetched audits are old and not from the recognized-firm list used for green.
steelman.green: The green case is that the core proxy, implementation, governance, Delegator, and ProxyAdmin ABIs/sources are publicly available and at least one broad audit covered the relevant repository files.

rationale.verdict: Choosing orange because verifiability is materially better than red due verified deployed sources, public repos, and fetched audits, but weaker than green because the current implementation page flags unverified Poseidon libraries, no current deployment commit match was pinned, and the fetched audits are stale relative to current verified deployments.

protocol_metadata.about: Railgun lets users shield ERC20/ERC721 assets into an on-chain zero-knowledge privacy system and later spend, transfer, interact with DeFi, or unshield through transact. The core user actions are shield and transact, with private balances represented by encrypted notes in a shared Merkle tree and SNARK-verified spends. Optional broadcasters can relay private transactions for UX/privacy, but the SDK and contracts expose direct contract-interaction paths.
